More Singapore occupiers planning to increase office space; AI impact on demand still unclear: CBRE survey
article:
More companies in Singapore are expecting to expand their office space over the next three years, a CBRE survey has found.

The firm’s 2026 Asia Pacific (Apac) Office Occupier Survey , which surveyed 651 respondents across the region between May 27 and July 10, found that 50% are looking to grow their office footprint, up from 32% in the past three years, amid an increase in office attendance.

Singapore follows the same pattern, with 41% of the 18 Singapore respondents polled expecting to expand their office space over the next three years, up from 29% in the past three years. About 71% are targeting office space in CBD locations, while 76% prefer Grade A buildings.

The higher proportion points to “renewed confidence in the role of the office as a platform for growth”, said Tricia Song, CBRE’s head of research for Singapore and Southeast Asia.

“Compared with three years ago, a significantly higher proportion of companies are planning to expand their office footprint, supported by consistently strong workplace attendance and a clear preference for CBD locations and Grade A buildings," she added.

About 94% of Singapore respondents said their staff now attends the office at least three days per week, higher than the 75% indicated last year. Office attendance is now the highest since the pandemic, CBRE added.

Singapore’s office attendance rate outpaces the wider Apac region, with 88% of all survey respondents indicating staff spend at least three days in the office.

While optimisation of existing office space continues to be a priority for Apac occupiers, CBRE noted that utilisation is being balanced with the need to provide an attractive workplace experience.

While more companies have opted for unassigned seating over fixed desk arrangements, sharing ratios have largely plateaued at the 1 to 1.5 range, down from previously prevalent ratios exceeding two staff to one desk.

In addition, occupiers are leaning towards larger workstations, reversing a shrinkage of desk sizes observed in Apac in recent years. About 42% of the survey’s respondents indicated a preferred desk size of over 100 sq ft, higher than the 35% recorded in 2024.

In Singapore, 75% of respondents want to keep desk sharing ratios below 1:1.5, while 53% expect workstation size to be above 100 sq ft.

CBRE’s survey also highlighted that despite growing AI adoption, the impact on office demand remains unclear. Over half (56%) of respondents across Apac believe AI will have no meaningful impact on their office footprint or consider it too early to make an assessment.

In Singapore, that segment is even higher, at 65%. In addition, 24% of Singapore respondents believe more office space will be required due to AI adoption.

title: JustCo hits 60 operational centres, another 11 in the pipeline
article:
JustCo Holdings opened 10 new centres in the first nine months of 2026. This included centres in three new markets: India, Malaysia and the Philippines.

This brings its number of operational centres to 60, the Singapore Exchange -listed flexible workspace provider said in its latest business update, published on Nov 24.

The group’s blended occupancy for the first nine months stood at 79%. Centres that opened before 2026 have an occupancy of 84%, while centres that opened in 2026 have an occupancy of 23%.

JustCo Holdings, whose brands include JustCo, The Collective and The Boring Office, has a further pipeline of 11 centres set to open over the next 12 months, five of which are in Singapore.

They comprise a new floor at Central Plaza on Tiong Bahru Road, where the group already has an existing JustCo, along with new centres at The Octagon and Raffles City.

It is also slated to unveil the retail podium at JustCo Place , a co-working, co-living and retail development at 160 Orchard Road in December. The co-working component was completed in September, and is fully leased by Deloitte Singapore.

The co-living spaces, comprising 123 units that will be operated under a new Just At brand, will be ready next year.  The co-living units range from studios to three-bedroom spaces.

Despite the group’s ongoing expansions, JustCo Holdings’ cash balance stood at US$167 million (about $216 million) as of Sept 30, an increase from US$104 million as at Dec 31, 2025. It is also remains Cash ebitda positive, the group added.

title: 'AI talent war' to support rental demand for private housing: Realion
article:
The private residential rental market is expected to see steady demand in 2027, backed by AI-related expat talent seeking homes.

Total leasing volume for the private housing market is expected to range between 90,000 to 95,000 units next year, comparable to the 93,000 to 95,000 leases estimated for 2026, Realion (OrangeTee & ETC) Group said in a November research report.

It estimates private home rents to climb 3% to 4% next year, up from 2.5% to 3% in 2026.

Realion’s upbeat outlook for the private housing rental market comes amid an “AI talent war” that has driven up skilled professional compensation.

As the AI industry has seen a boom in investments, more high-net-worth individuals have emerged, resulting in a pool of “AI-elite, high-income tenants” entering the rental market, Realion said.

At the same time, rental housing supply is expected to increase in coming years, largely due to more HDB flats achieving their five-year minimum occupation period (MOP). Realion estimates almost 100,000 flats will reach their MOP between 2026 and 2030.

“The supply increase will impact both private and public markets, since many new flats offer desirable attributes, such as good connectivity and design features, that appeal to a wider audience,” the report added.

Private housing supply will also increase, with Realion projecting the number of new private homes completions to jump from around 7,783 units in 2026 to 8,858 units in 2027, excluding executive condos.

Despite the bump up in rental housing supply, Realion expects the AI-driven increase in the tenant pool, coupled with limited supply of prime residences, to support leasing demand for private homes next year.

On the other hand, rental demand for HDB flats, especially smaller units, could ease in 2027. “As the government continues to launch more BTO flats and speed up construction of existing ones, some local households or tenants may move from renting to owner-occupation, reducing the pool of local tenants,” Realion explained.

Another factor that may impact the rental market is the completion of the Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System Link next year. The enhanced cross-border connectivity could prompt some tenants, especially those in the north, to relocate to Johor Bahru due to lower housing costs.

Realion is projecting HDB leasing volume of 32,000 to 35,000 in 2027, down from 36,000 to 38,000 in 2026. It anticipates HDB rents to move between -1% and 2% for next year.

title: Do You Sell When Your Small-Cap Grows into a Large-Cap?
article:
Every investor dreams of finding an overlooked
small-cap gem
and watching it blossom into a market giant.
Yet, when that dream actually comes true, it creates a surprising dilemma: should you take the money and run?
When you invest in a small company, you do so hoping to watch it expand.
Selling halfway along its journey simply because it outgrows its small-cap label makes little sense.
Why Did the Stock Cross S$1 Billion?
In Singapore, small-caps are typically defined as businesses with a market capitalisation under S$1 billion.
When one of your holdings crosses that threshold, your next move depends on why its value climbed.
Sometimes, a stock breaches the S$1 billion mark purely due to temporary market exuberance rather than underlying business progress.
When enthusiasm inflates a
valuation
beyond what is justified, you can simply sit tight and see if the share price settles back down.
On the other hand, if the company crossed S$1 billion because its operations genuinely expanded – and it has the potential to reach S$2 billion or more in the years ahead – you should let it keep running.
If you manage a dedicated small-cap portfolio and want to keep its focus pure, you do not have to hit the sell button.
Simply transfer that graduating stock into a separate portfolio without small-cap constraints, allowing it to keep compounding there.
Starting with one portfolio and eventually managing two because your winners outgrew the first is a wonderful problem to have.
Elephants, Fleas, and Growing Up
A common argument for selling is that elephants do not gallop, whereas fleas can jump thousands of times their own size.
Once a small company matures into a large-cap, its percentage growth rate naturally slows down.
Think of it like raising a child.
When a baby is born, they grow at an astonishing pace.
If you projected that infant growth rate forward indefinitely, you would assume you needed a ten-foot bed by the time they hit their teens.
Eventually, growth tapers off – not because anything is wrong, but because the child is maturing and developing new strengths.
Companies follow the exact same lifecycle.
Early on, revenue and profits surge rapidly.
As the business matures, growth moderates, yet the company often becomes more resilient and continues rewarding shareholders with
reliable dividends
.
While some investors prefer to cash out at S$1 billion to hunt for the next small-cap, holding on means keeping a proven, cash-generative business in your corner.
Get Smart: Conviction Beats Market Volatility
Outgrowing the small-cap label is a happy problem, not a reason to panic.
If you have done your homework and found a business capable of evolving into a market leader, you have already conquered the hardest part of investing – don’t discard a proven compounding machine just to chase an unproven gamble.

title: Anthropic breaks below US$83 IPO price in premarket trading
article:
(Nov 24): Anthropic PBC shares traded below the US$83 IPO price in premarket trading, wiping out gains for investors who piled into the artificial intelligence lab’s record-setting debut.

The stock declined as much as 7.3% to US$81.28 per share as of 6.15am on Tuesday (Nov 24) in New York. The company's shares have been volatile, soaring briefly above US$100 on their first trading day following its initial public offering as investors cheered the arrival of a listed frontier AI firm.

Concerns over the pace of spending on the controversial technology roiled stocks even as bankers were working hard to lift the amount of money raised by the Claude chatbot maker’s debut above SpaceX’s record fundraise. Anthropic’s IPO was multiple times oversubscribed, with well over US$500 billion of demand translating into a US$119.5 billion haul for the company and its seven co-founders.

Anthropic’s IPO left more than half of the institutional investors bidding for stock without any shares, with allocations heavily skewed toward US-based investors, Bloomberg News reported. About 1,200 institutional investors placed orders, people familiar with the matter have said.

The rapid adoption of products such as Claude Code, Anthropic’s coding agent for software developers, and the company’s revenue run rate of US$81 billion at the end of October made for a powerful sales pitch. That helped investors overlook the company’s committed spending nearing US$901 billion through 2045.

SpaceX shares climbed as much as 67% above the IPO price before falling below it less than five weeks after its debut. A company’s shares sinking below that mark in the first few months of trading represents a blow to the narrative bankers have carefully constructed during the marketing. Some newly listed companies’ stock prices do not recover from breaching that important level.

See also: Zoom seeks Asia Pacific growth with AI beyond meetings

Anthropic and its rival OpenAI face mounting public scrutiny over AI safety after a string of high-profile hacking incidents by rogue agents, and the debate rages over whether the technology poses what Anthropic called “existential risks to humanity” in its IPO filing. OpenAI has filed confidentially for a listing but is not planning to go public before 2027.

title: Boeing wins US$7.4 bil order in biggest China buy in years
article:
(Nov 24): Boeing Co received a US$7.4 billion order for 50 single-aisle jets from a unit of China Southern Airlines Co, the country’s first major purchase from the US manufacturer in years.

The order will consist entirely of 737-8 Max planes, the unit, Xiamen Airlines Co, said in an exchange filing Tuesday (Nov 24).

The order follows through on a commitment this year by China to buy hundreds of Boeing aircraft. On Monday, US President Donald Trump said he expected China to buy 250 more jets.

Boeing, one of America’s largest exporters by dollar value, has been frozen out of China as it battles a string of production- and quality-related challenges, mostly stemming from major accidents. This deal marks Boeing’s biggest order from Chinese airlines since 2017.

China had previously agreed to buy 200 planes, making a commitment back in May during Trump’s state visit to China. However, Beijing has not formalised a deal. The tentative agreement fell well short at the time of the expected order for 500 jets, both single-aisle and widebody models.

Washington and Beijing have been locked in a long-running trade war, ranging from critical minerals to semiconductor chips. Trump has leveraged trade and used tariffs to secure favourable deals for American companies and Boeing has been a major beneficiary.

See also: Japan pledges financial support for International Criminal Court

For the past decade, China placed orders for several hundred Airbus SE aircraft and its domestic airlines supplemented them by agreeing to buy hundreds of rival homegrown Commercial Aircraft Corp of China Ltd planes.

China is the second-biggest aviation market and is expected to surpass the US in the next decade, according to industry forecasts.

Xiamen Air has a fleet of 174 aircraft, according to Planespotters.net and also has several dozen planes on order, mostly from Airbus.

title: Subprime auto dealer America’s Car-Mart files for Chapter 11
article:
(Nov 24): America’s Car-Mart Inc, a used-car seller and subprime lender, filed for bankruptcy to sell the business under court supervision.

The Rogers, Arkansas-based company filed for Chapter 11 in the Southern District of Texas on Tuesday, court documents showed. It listed assets of US$100 million to US$500 million and liabilities of US$1 billion to US$10 billion in its petition.

America’s Car-Mart is one of the best known in the “buy here, pay here” segment of auto finance, where companies operate their own dealerships and provide financing to customers in-house. The sector caters to “deep” subprime borrowers who often can’t obtain financing elsewhere.

Once a market darling of the Covid pandemic era, the cash-strapped company has come under pressure after interest rate hikes put an end to ultra-cheap borrowing. In June, America’s Car-Mart defaulted on a US$300 million term loan from Silver Point Capital to repay its asset-backed line of credit and had been operating under short-dated forbearance extensions. It listed total debts of US$624 million in its earnings report for the first quarter that ended July 31.

The company has struggled to emerge from its performance rut, constrained by reduced inventory and limited capacity to write new loans. It reported revenue of US$146 million in the first quarter, a 57% plunge from the year-ago period. Meanwhile, the value of its inventory fell 35% from the prior three months, as the company curtailed new purchases and sold its vehicles in order to preserve liquidity.

title: LME to list major new aluminium brand as historic squeeze deepens
article:
(Nov 24): The London Metal Exchange is preparing to authorise deliveries of aluminium from a major new smelter in Indonesia into its warehousing network, offering potential supply relief as a historic squeeze roils the global market.

The LME is in the final stages of authorising metal produced by PT Hua Chin Aluminium Indonesia for delivery against its contracts, following on from its brand application in May, according to people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified because the registration is still being finalised.

Hua Chin is one of several new smelters being built and ramped up in Indonesia, and the 480,000-tonne-a-year plant could help to alleviate inventory shortages and pricing pressures on the LME that have exposed the global aluminium industry to heavy losses.

Spot aluminium prices on the LME have traded at huge premiums to later-dated futures over recent days, moving into the biggest backwardation since an infamous squeeze in the 1980s. The ructions have come as LME inventories have slumped to the lowest level since 1990, with surging output in Indonesia bringing little relief so far because only one of the country’s smelters produces LME-deliverable metal.

title: Ex-RBI chief Rajan sees Nvidia governance risk with return of Huang
article:
(Nov 24): Jensen Huang’s surprise return to lead Nvidia Corp puts a spotlight on corporate governance and the company’s pivotal role in the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, according to former Reserve Bank of India (RBI) governor Raghuram Rajan.

Rajan, a finance professor at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business, said the global rally that followed also raised questions about the US government’s role in putting him back in charge, and governance at Nvidia under his renewed leadership.

“Are there going to be checks and balances on him?” Rajan said in an interview with Bloomberg Television’s Haslinda Amin. He asked whether potential malfeasance would be thoroughly investigated by the US chipmaker.

Huang’s return to the company at the centre of the AI boom restored confidence in technology stocks after his exit earlier this month rattled the trade. But Rajan said a larger question that predated the latest turmoil remains: whether returns on trillions of dollars of investment in computing can justify the debt-fuelled spending.

Rajan said some people compare Nvidia to American International Group Inc during the 2008 global financial crisis because it sits at the centre of many contracts and helps keep the boom going. He said the systemic risk isn’t significant now but could grow given the scale of planned investment.

Rajan stopped short of calling AI a bubble, saying it may simply reflect excessive optimism. He said security concerns, particularly in the event of a major cyberattack, could trigger a sharp drop in demand.

See also: Australia bolsters online safety law with tougher Big Tech fine

title: German business outlook improves for seventh straight month
article:
(Nov 24): Germany’s business outlook improved for a seventh month, cementing hopes that the economy has finally overcome years of stagnation.

An expectations index by the Ifo institute rose to 91.9 in November from a revised 91.5 the previous month, almost matching the median estimate in a Bloomberg survey of 92. A measure of current conditions also advanced.

“The recovery of the German economy is proceeding, but it lacks breadth,” Ifo president Clemens Fuest said on Tuesday in a statement that described improvements for services and trade, while manufacturing and construction suffered setbacks.

Europe’s biggest economy has performed much more strongly than expected when the Iran war broke out in February. Large-scale government spending is providing a tailwind, as are exports, underpinned by the investment boom in artificial intelligence.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s economic advisers have more than doubled their forecast for GDP growth to 1.3% this year and 1% in 2027. Such optimism has been backed up by indicators including S&P Global’s Purchasing Managers Index, which unexpectedly surged to its highest level in more than four and a half years in November.

See also: Australia to lower nominal economy estimate in budget update

Inflation remains a concern, with the Bundesbank predicting price gains will pick up at the start of 2027 as a temporary fuel rebate expires. There’s also concern that low gas-storage levels could lead to a price spike in case of a cold winter.

Elsewhere, the European Central Bank is set to raise interest rates for the third time this year in December, taking them into territory where they may act as a brake on growth. Some policymakers have said further tightening is possible.

title: China extends pause on US minerals ban to maintain truce
article:
(Nov 24): China extended the suspension of a ban on exports of several critical minerals to the US, preserving a key element of a fragile trade truce despite growing tensions over technology.

China’s Commerce Ministry on Tuesday kept the ban on US-bound shipments of gallium, germanium and antimony on hold through Jan 27, prolonging a suspension that was due to expire Friday. The materials are used in products ranging from semiconductors to satellites and military equipment.

The extension follows last week’s summit between Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping in Shenzhen and comes hours after the US president helped secure the reinstatement of Jensen Huang, a vocal opponent to stringent chip export controls, as the chief of Nvidia Corp on Monday.

But Washington has also tightened restrictions on China’s access to advanced artificial intelligence chips through overseas data centres. If fully enforced, the measures could hamper Beijing’s efforts to catch up with the US in AI.

The US Commerce Department announced the new rules just days before the summit. China’s Commerce Ministry said the restrictions violated understandings reached by the two leaders and warned of countermeasures if Washington presses ahead.

China first imposed the US-specific critical minerals ban in December 2024 in retaliation against the Biden administration’s widening chip curbs. It suspended its enforcement last November after Trump and Xi struck a trade truce in South Korea, setting Nov 27, 2026, as the expiration date.

See also: China stockpiles soyoil as domestic prices hit three-month low

The extension brings the suspension into line with other elements of the truce that run through January, including tariff relief and a pause on additional Chinese export controls on rare earths that are set to expire on Jan 10.

China’s dominance of critical mineral supply chains proved a powerful source of leverage in last year’s trade war, when Beijing’s export controls helped pressure Washington to back down.

China accounts for 99% of global production of primary low-purity gallium, about 80% of natural graphite output, and 36% of mined antimony, according to US Geological Survey estimates for 2025. The agency also identified China as the leading global producer and exporter of germanium metal in 2025, without specify its share.

title: JPMorgan and HSBC trade digital gold in London for first time
article:
(Nov 24): JPMorgan Chase & Co and other major precious metals dealers traded a new form of digital gold in London for the first time, an early test of a system that could revamp the plumbing of the world’s biggest bullion hub.

JPMorgan, HSBC Holdings plc and StoneX Group Inc completed their first trades using fractional ownership interests in physical gold bars last week, the World Gold Council industry group said in a statement. While still at a trial stage, a successful rollout of the new system could mark one of the most significant additions to the structure of the London bullion market in decades.

“This is a historic step forward for the gold market,” said David Tait, chief executive officer of the WGC, which led the initiative. “For the first time, leading institutions have transferred, settled and used fractional ownership of physical gold as collateral through real, live transactions.”

Hundreds of billions of dollars worth of gold change hands every week in London, setting benchmark prices for the global precious metals industry. What is traded in that market, for the most part, are “unallocated” paper contracts that oblige the vaulting bank to deliver gold on request.

Trading unallocated gold is cheaper and easier than transacting in hefty 400 ounce bars, allowing traders to pay lower storage fees and deal in precise quantities of metal. The drawbacks are that holders remain exposed to the creditworthiness of the vaulting bank, and that the paper claims cannot generally be used as collateral.

See also: Gold extends gain after Nvidia’s rehiring of Huang sparks rally

Banks can post the new fractional gold — called ‘pooled gold interests’ — as collateral without needing to move the physical metal, potentially making bullion a more useful financial asset. The WGC is also lobbying UK authorities to bring gold within the country’s financial-collateral regime, which would make it easier to pledge and enforce in insolvency.

Gold that is fractional, easily transferable and shielded from the insolvency of an intermediary would allow the metal “to be used more widely across financial markets, including as collateral”, Mark Amlin, global head of physical commodities at JPMorgan, said in the statement.

Asian financial centres are looking to capture a greater share of bullion trading from London. Hong Kong began trial operations of a new gold clearing system similar to London’s this year, while Singapore unveiled measures including a gold vaulting service for central banks.

See also: Gold rebounds as tech rout spurs shift to havens, Treasury rally

Earlier this year, the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority sought the views of the financial sector on gold tokenization, adding that developing the next generation of gold-market infrastructure would “reinforce and preserve London’s position as a centre for gold trading and custody”.

With well over US$1 trillion ($1.29 trillion) worth of gold in its vaults, including mounds of central bank-owned metal underneath the Bank of England, London is unlikely to lose its position as the dominant trading hub anytime soon. Many traders also expect the market will probably maintain its primarily “unallocated” structure, even if pooled gold interests prove to be popular with dealers and clients.

Not all prior attempts to reform London’s precious metals market have been successful. Four years ago, the London Metal Exchange abandoned an effort to move more trading onto an exchange, an initiative backed by banks including Goldman Sachs Group Inc and Morgan Stanley, after the contracts failed to attract sufficient volumes.

Unlike some previous attempts to reshape London’s bullion market, pooled gold interests are designed to work alongside the existing over-the-counter system, rather than shift trading away from it, said Mike Oswin, global head of market structure at the WGC. “We are not here to say the unallocated market isn’t working,” Oswin said. “This is complementary to it.”

Several elements still need to be worked out before pooled gold interests can be rolled out more broadly, he added, including deciding how the system would be governed.

Five banks currently provide vaulting and oversee the existing clearing infrastructure in the London market: Citigroup Inc, ICBC Standard Bank, UBS Group AG, HSBC, and the biggest player, JPMorgan. Deutsche Bank AG and Morgan Stanley are also seeking to join the small club, Bloomberg reported in October.
